newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: OTC day trade to boost Portugal bond market.
newsitem.headline: OTC day trade to boost Portugal bond market.

text.p: Turnover and efficiency on Portugal's bond market will increase following the approval of day trade on the Over The Counter (OTC) market, analysts said.
The Financial Markets Committee (CMVM) approved a regulation on Thursday which permits day trade in public debt on the OTC market.
The new regulation, which will allow buying and selling of the same debt instrument in one day, will become effective on the day after its publication in the Lisbon bourse bulletin.
"With the approval of day trade, there will be an increase in the liquidity and depth of the market, which will make it more efficient," said Nuno Godinho, analyst of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Analysts said the introduction of day trade, as well as plans to improve regulations to encourage short selling and a more efficient repo market, would attract increasing numbers of foreign investors to the market.

Serge Goncalves of Royal Bank of Scotland in London said: "The approval of day trade will help Portugal's public debt market to develop and is decisive to attract institutional investors, especially from Europe and the U.S."
Luis Pina of Banco ESSI said: "What the foreigners want is liquidity and volatility, i.e. an efficient market, and day trade is an important step in that direction."
A fixed income analyst said: "After the introduction of day trade, domestic investors will open up their portfolios much more, there will be more paper in the market and much greater volatility."

One analyst with an international investment bank in London said: "The cash market could have a boom because not just the banks, but also the funds and insurance companies will do much more trading, and it will be much easier to get into and out of the market.

"Portuguese bonds will follow much more closely the volatility in foreign markets. We could increase our exposure (to the Portuguese bond market) because there is a lot of money to be made before (the launch of) the euro."

The stock of Portuguese fixed rate bonds is superior to 3,000 billion escudos, and analysts estimate that about eight percent is held by foreign investors, down from 11.8 percent in 1996 and 9.8 percent in 1995.
Yield spreads against 10-year Bunds have dropped to around 69 basis points (bp) from 320 bp in March 1996 as investors bet that Portugal will join the European single currency from the start in 1999.
